title: Industrial stocks: how to analyze industrial companies
description: Industrial stocks run on the cycle: order intake, margins through the cycle and the aftermarket moat — the method with worked examples and sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Industrial stocks are shares in companies that make machines, equipment and tools or build infrastructure — Stockholm's sector backbone: AB Volvo, ABB, Atlas Copco, Sandvik, SKF, Alfa Laval, Hexagon and Skanska, with American GE Aerospace and Eaton in AK1A's analysis universe. Most share one trait: demand arrives in waves — when the world invests, business is good; when the economy turns, order intake falls first, profits after. The cycle is the sector's first analytical fact — and the reason industrial stocks get their own method.

The numbers are unexpected: the industrial sector's median P/E in the universe is 28, against the universe's 20.2, with the EBIT margin at 16.9 percent, the FCF margin at 10.8 percent and revenue growth at 8.4 percent (raw data 2026-09-15). The "cheap cyclical sector" painted by finance literature does not match today's universe — modern industry is high technology with moats. This guide walks through the cycle, the margins, the aftermarket's role and the multiple — with worked examples and sources. As always: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are industrial stocks — three kinds of businesses

The industrial label holds several businesses; the sorting decides which measures matter.

- **Capital goods and heavy technology.** Volvo, ABB and Sandvik sell trucks, robot systems and machines to other companies — sales follow customers' investment budgets and the economy with amplification.
- **Industrial technology with an aftermarket.** Alfa Laval, Atlas Copco, ASSA ABLOY, SKF and Hexagon deliver products where service, spare parts and software recur long after the first sale — a revenue base smoothing the cycle.
- **Construction.** Skanska's revenues follow building norms and public procurement — a cycle of its own, partly independent of the capital goods cycle.

A fourth category is no industry at all: Industrivärden is an investment company owning shares in Sandvik and Ericsson among others — analyzed on its net asset calculation, not on order cycles. The difference between owning a manufacturer and owning an owner of manufacturers is covered in [Investment companies](/kurser/km-067-investmentbolag), with an example in [the Industrivärden analysis](/blogg/analys-industrivarden-2026). The overview's numbers are in [the sector medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2), and [the Industrial Sector](/kurser/km-041-industrisektorn) covers the sector systematically.

## The cycle — order intake leads the income statement

Industry's fuel is order intake: new orders divided by invoiced revenue. A company invoicing SEK 10 billion and taking new orders worth SEK 11 billion stands at 1.1 — the order book grows and the production calendar fills. The measure is often called book-to-bill; above 1.0 the order book grows, below 1.0 it drains. Order intake is published monthly or quarterly and turns months before the income statement — industry's early warning system. The cycle's portfolio consequences are covered in [Cycle risk](/kurser/rk-05-cykelrisk).

Worth memorizing: order intake turns first, then capacity utilization, then margins — profit last. Capacity utilization explains the margin swing: when orders rise at a factory with idle capacity, production increases without new costs and the margin rises faster than revenue; full utilization instead requires investments in new capacity — spending that arrives before the revenue. That is why industry's margins swing harder than its volumes. A worked example: a company invoicing SEK 10 billion at a 15 percent EBIT margin earns SEK 1.5 billion at the top. In the downturn, volume falls 15 percent and the margin is pressed to 8 percent — the result becomes SEK 8.5 billion × 8 percent ≈ SEK 0.7 billion. More than half the profit vanished on a volume and margin move that looks innocent in percent.

## The margin through the cycle — the P/E trap explained

Here lives the sector's classic trap, deserving a full calculation. A cyclical company at the peak: earnings per share SEK 12, price SEK 240 — the P/E becomes 240 ÷ 12 = 20. Two years later, at the cycle's bottom, earnings stand at SEK 6 and the price at SEK 180 — the P/E becomes 180 ÷ 6 = 30. The "cheap" company (P/E 20) was expensive, and the "expensive" one (P/E 30) may be near its cheapest point on a cycle-adjusted basis. For cyclical companies the P/E is read through the cycle, not at a single date — and complemented with [EV/EBIT](/kurser/km-010-evebit), which weighs in the debt, or the company's own margin history: is today's margin near the cycle top's 15 percent or the bottom's 8 percent? The margin's position in the cycle is the question; the multiple is only input.

## The aftermarket — the moat that smooths

The cycle is not the whole truth: the share of revenues from the aftermarket — service, spare parts, consumables, software licenses — decides how hard the downturn strikes. The logic: whoever owns the machine must maintain it even in a recession, and service revenue often carries a higher margin than new sales. A company with 40 percent aftermarket revenue dampens its cycle tilt automatically; a company with 5 percent stands naked in the same downturn. The measure and its analysis: [Revenue stability](/blogg/v12-intaktsstabilitet-analys). In practice the aftermarket share sits in the segment information — look for service, aftermarket and recurring in the report; there lies the moat, or its absence.

## The multiple — more expensive than the rumor

The median P/E of 28 against the universe's 20.2 is the sector's most surprising number, and the explanation is structural: the universe's industrial companies are not steel mills but technology companies in disguise — Hexagon measures the world with software, Atlas Copco sells compressed air as a service, ASSA locks doors with digital systems. The quartile spread 18.2–35.8 shows the tension between classic capital goods and technology-heavy manufacturing. The P/B of 4.9 says the same thing: the value lives in knowledge, brands and installed base — not in machine halls. The consequence: compare each company with its own group within the sector and its own history five years back; a shared "industry normal" no longer exists.

## The balance sheet in the downturn

The cycle's third leg is financing. A highly indebted company enters the downturn with less room to maneuver: interest eats the margin buffer while profit falls. The basic measures are as always — [debt-to-equity ratio](/blogg/vad-ar-skuldsattningsgrad) and net debt relative to EBITDA — but the interpretation is cyclical: calculate the debt measures if EBIT falls 40 percent. That stress test separates companies that catch their breath in the downturn from those forced to the emission table.

## How to read the industrial report

Five details worth extra attention. First, order intake and the order book — relative to invoiced, geography visible: an order book growing in Asia but shrinking in Europe is a different story than the reverse. Second, the margin per segment — mining equipment and construction cycle differently. Third, receivables and inventory: they swing with the cycle and can reveal sales pulled forward. Fourth, currencies — larger Swedish industrial companies often report in dollars and euros; currency moves can hide both growth and decline. Fifth, management's outlook against the previous report's: revised forecasts into a downturn are information about the cycle position. The reading order of [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) and [How to read a Swedish annual report](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-svensk-arsredovisning) is the framework — a concrete example: [how we analyzed Volvo Cars](/blogg/hur-vi-analyserade-volvo-cars).

## The summary

- Sort the business: capital goods, technology with an aftermarket, or construction — and sort out investment companies sitting in the sector.
- Order intake leads: book-to-bill above 1.0 means the order book grows; order intake turns months before the profits.
- The P/E is read through the cycle: in the example the P/E was 20 at the top and 30 at the bottom — same company, two years.
- The aftermarket share is the moat: 40 percent service revenue dampens the cycle sharply.
- Median P/E 28 against the universe's 20.2: today's industry is technology companies — compare within the group, not against an old "cheap" reputation.

Next step: [the Industrial Sector](/kurser/km-041-industrisektorn) deepens the sector, [Cycle risk](/kurser/rk-05-cykelrisk) the economic mechanics, and [EV/EBIT](/kurser/km-010-evebit) the multiple that works when the P/E fails.
